passages.happening:
Saul comes back from fighting the Philistines and hears that David is in the wilderness of En-gedi. He takes three thousand chosen men to hunt for him near the Rocks of the Wild Goats (verses 1-2).

Saul comes to the sheepfolds by the road, where there is a cave, and goes in to relieve himself. David and his men are hiding deep inside the same cave (verse 3).

David's men say that this is the day the LORD promised, when he would give David's enemy into his hand. David creeps up and cuts off a corner of Saul's robe (verse 4). ‘Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe’ (verse 5).

“The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD’s anointed. May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed” (verse 6). With these words David holds his men back and does not let them attack Saul. Saul leaves the cave and goes on his way (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The last chapter ended with David narrowly escaping Saul and going to En-gedi. Now the hunter is at the mercy of the hunted. This is the first of two times David spares Saul's life. The second is in chapter 26. Together they show that David will not take the throne by violence. He has been anointed, but he will wait for God to give him the kingdom.

En-gedi is an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, fed by springs that fall from steep cliffs. The wilderness around it is full of caves, and wild goats still live there. Sheepfolds were often built at the mouths of caves, and some caves there are large enough to hide many men in their inner depths.

Saul brings three thousand chosen men, as many as he kept with him in chapter 13, against David's six hundred.

The corner of a robe meant more than a modern reader expects. The edge of a garment could stand for the wearer's identity and authority. Cutting a piece from the king's robe was a symbolic act against his royal standing, and that is why David's conscience troubles him even for this. It also recalls the robe Saul tore in chapter 15, when Samuel said the LORD had torn the kingdom from him.

David's men call it the LORD's day of opportunity. David calls Saul the LORD's anointed. Though God has rejected Saul, the anointing still marks him as set apart, and David will not raise his hand against it.
passages.later: Two psalm headings set prayers in a cave while David fled from Saul: ‘A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul into the cave’ (Psalm 57:1), and ‘A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave’ (Psalm 142:1). The headings do not say which cave.
passages.hard:
Is David's respect for ‘the LORD’s anointed’ a teaching that leaders should never be opposed, even when they do wrong?

Some have used this chapter to argue that people in authority, especially religious or political leaders, may never be criticized or resisted. That reading goes further than the text. David does refuse to kill Saul. But he also confronts him openly, calls on God to judge him, and runs rather than submit to his unjust demands.

Readers disagree on how far the principle reaches. Some take it narrowly, as a refusal to use violence against the king God had anointed. Others see a broader respect for authority that still allows truth-telling, flight and appeal to God. The prophets of the Old Testament often confronted kings, and the New Testament teaches both respect for authorities and obedience to God over people when the two conflict. What the chapter teaches is restraint and trust in God's timing, not silence before injustice.

And nothing in this passage shields a leader who does harm. Christians agree that leaders are servants accountable to Christ and to his word, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse. If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David's men said, ‘This is the day’, and David said no. Ask when you have been handed a chance to get even and called it God's will. And ask what it would mean to leave your cause with God, without keeping silent about what is wrong.

passages.t: ‘May the LORD judge between you and me’
passages.happening:
David goes out of the cave after Saul and calls, “My lord the king!” When Saul looks back, David bows to the ground (verse 8).

He asks why Saul listens to people who say David means to harm him. Today the LORD gave Saul into his hand in the cave. He was told to kill him, but he spared him (verses 9-10). ‘See, my father, look at the corner of your robe in my hand. For I cut it off, but I did not kill you’ (verse 11). There is no evil or rebellion in his hands, he says, though Saul is hunting him down to take his life.

“May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you” (verse 12). As the old saying goes, ‘Wickedness proceeds from the wicked’ (verse 13). Whom is the king of Israel chasing? ‘A dead dog? A flea?’ (verse 14). David asks the LORD to judge, to plead his case and to rescue him (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The first half of the chapter was quick and tense, with almost no words from David except his refusal. Now David speaks at length.

He calls Saul ‘my father’. It is a mark of respect, and a reminder that David is Saul's son-in-law. A dead dog and a flea were common ways of calling oneself worthless, of saying that the king was wasting his power on someone who was no threat.

The word hand binds the chapter together. David's men say God has put Saul into David's hand. David says again and again that his hand will not be against Saul. He shows Saul the corner of the robe, in his hand, as proof.

Three times David calls on God as judge. The word for judge covers both deciding a dispute and rescuing the innocent party. David hands vengeance over to God instead of taking it himself.
passages.later:
The law says that vengeance belongs to God: ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay’ (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Paul gives the same rule to Christians: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19).

Many readers have thought of this day when reading a psalm of David that protests his innocence: ‘if I have rewarded my ally with evil, if I have plundered my foe without cause’ (Psalm 7:4). The psalm itself does not name the moment.
passages.asks: David showed Saul the piece of the robe in his hand as proof that he meant no harm. Ask how you could show someone who fears you that you will not repay them. And ask whether you have handed your own case over to God, or are still trying to win it yourself.

passages.happening:
“Is that your voice, David my son?” Saul asks, and he weeps aloud (verse 16). “You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil” (verse 17). When the LORD gave him into David's hand, David did not kill him. ‘When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go away unharmed?’ (verse 19).

“Now I know for sure that you will be king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands” (verse 20). Saul asks David to swear by the LORD that he will not cut off Saul's descendants or wipe out his name from his father's house (verse 21).

David gives his oath. Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Saul's words state the lesson of the story. David has repaid evil with good. Saul says it, weeping.

For the first time Saul says openly what he has feared since chapter 18: David will be king. The kingdom will indeed be established in David's hands, after Saul's death.

Saul's request echoes Jonathan's in chapter 20. A new king commonly wiped out the family of the old one, so Saul asks for his descendants' lives. David swears, and he will keep his word.

But notice where they go. Saul goes home. David goes back up to the stronghold. He does not trust Saul's tears, and he is right not to. Chapter 26 will show that Saul's repentance did not last. A confession made in the heat of the moment, however sincere, is not the same as a lasting change.
passages.later:
In time the elders of all Israel came to David at Hebron, ‘And they anointed him king over Israel’ (2 Samuel 5:3).

Proverbs commends what David did: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink” (Proverbs 25:21).
passages.asks: Saul wept and confessed, and then went home unchanged. Ask whether your own tears over wrong have led to a change in what you do. And ask how you can forgive someone, as David did, without putting yourself back in their power.
